Ambiguous

/am-BIG-yoo-us/ — stress on second syllable, like big-YOU-us · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something that is ambiguous can be understood in more than one way, so its exact meaning stays unclear.

The note said only 'meet at the bank' — ambiguous, since the river and the ATM were both nearby.

Worked Example

The coach said 'You should work on your game' — ambiguous, since it could mean 'You're strong but need to push harder' or 'You're underperforming.'

Ambiguous is more precise than 'unclear' because it captures not just difficulty understanding, but the existence of multiple valid interpretations. The coach's words could legitimately mean two opposite things, and that's what ambiguous names.

How Ambiguous Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

unclear

unclear: not easy to understand or interpret

vague

vague: fuzzy and missing specific details

equivocal

equivocal: worded so it can be read two ways

Antonyms

explicit

explicit: stated so precisely only one reading fits

unequivocal

unequivocal: leaving absolutely no doubt about its meaning

How Strong Is It? — vague → equivocal → ambiguous → contradictory

vague vs. ambiguous

vague vs. ambiguous: Vague is milder than ambiguous: a vague statement is just fuzzy on details, while an ambiguous one actively points to two different meanings.

equivocal vs. ambiguous

equivocal vs. ambiguous: Equivocal is a step beyond ambiguous — an ambiguous remark happens to allow two readings, but an equivocal one is often worded that way on purpose to dodge commitment.

contradictory vs. ambiguous

contradictory vs. ambiguous: Contradictory is the strongest of the set: while an ambiguous message could mean either of two things, a contradictory one says two things that cannot both be true.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — amb-

Prefix — amb-: both, on both sides; around (Latin ambi-, shortened to amb- before a vowel)

Root — igu

Root — igu: to drive, move, go (from Latin agere, 'to drive'; inside ambiguus it is spelled -igu-)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of, having the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Amb- ('both ways, around') + igu ('to drive or move,' from Latin agere) + -ous ('full of') pictures a meaning that drives off in two directions at once — exactly why an ambiguous statement can be understood in more than one way, leaving its exact meaning unclear.

Use the root in a new word: agile

Use the root in a new word: agile: An agile dancer is quick to move and act — the same Latin root agere, 'to drive or move,' that pictures an ambiguous statement wandering back and forth between two meanings.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / neutral

Ambiguous is precise when something can reasonably be understood in two or more ways; use it when multiple interpretations are actually possible. If something is just unclear or vague, the simpler words are better. Save ambiguous for genuine cases—as in 'The sign was ambiguous, since it could mean both the store's name and its location.'
